title: Do you know any major directors who are incapable of portraying good female characters?

commenti.body:
Just because Jean Tatlock and Kitty Oppenheimer were supporting roles in the film doesnt mean they were poorly written

Murph in Interstellar is proof that when Nolan puts a female character at the front and centre of a movie, he can write good lead roles for women

wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount wordcount

Nolan was the first director to come to my mind. He makes men’s pictures. Women are used as props. With Interetellar he tries. But it’s still a male-centric circle jerk intended for men. He creates necessary but forgettable female characters. It’s the main reason I hate his films. He makes every female subservient, weak, incompetent. I honestly can’t watch his films again. He paints women as, “Gee thanks mister, thank goodness I had a man to help me out!” I find his treatment of female characters creepy and weird.

> The two main female characters in the film are skeletal and empty (as are almost all the characters in this film)

This line irked me coz if you yourself are admitting that the problems with Oppenheimer’s characters extend to all genders, then why use it as an example of Nolan’s inability to write women in particular? Most of his characters are kinda one-dimensional but I didn’t find e.g. Brand and Marv in Interstellar any worse than their male counterparts. 

> do you think that the inability to film half the population represents a major artistic limit for a filmmaker?

The broader thing with Nolan is that his movies are thematically and aesthetically very “male”, that’s the kind of stories he tells. He would absolutely suck at telling a more “female” story but I don’t feel like anyone wants one from him.

Nolan is the prime example of this. I’m not sure he’s ever properly talked with a woman in his life. 

I also think Zack Snyder qualifies. I still remember how he butchered the female characters in Superman and Watchmen.

I don’t know many directors who aren’t great with female characters to be honest.

Martin Scorsese has very fleshed out female characters, but a lot of them are very flawed, sometimes even terrible people.  But the same goes for his male characters, because that’s the kind of stories he tells.

The opposite answer to your question is James Cameron.  He is, in my opinion, one of the best male directors when it comes to writing female characters.  Ripley and Sarah Connor are two of the greatest female heroes ever written, and Rose, Neytiri, and just about every other female character Cameron’s ever written are all fully fleshed out, three-dimensional people who are just as vital to his stories as the men, sometimes even more.

I'm not talking about telling "female" stories. You can be a filmmaker telling stories seen as "male" and still have descent representations of female characters. Scorsese is the first that comes to mind.

I would argue that in Interstellar, he doesn’t. The lead character is Matthew. The women are there to try to help. But they’re painted as incompetent. He has to rescue them. He does the docking, he goes into the black hole. The women are just there as props. The director makes the story into a “the man saves the day” fest because the women weren’t smart enough. That maudlin final scene with the daughter is a good example. The director has the daughter be so incompetent that she could never figure it out and became old and Matthew had to figure everything out and see her on her deathbed. Nolan makes men’s pictures. It’s a genre. But he really can’t understand how to incorporate a strong, intelligent female character.

Plus, if you're unable to portray a particular type of character well, don't put them in your film, because this will result in characters playing important roles that are poorly constructed, and this is a flaw that will cast a pall over the whole film. But the problem is precisely that you're very limited in your choice of films if you do without half the population, which is why there are important female characters in some of his films (Nolan) even if he's telling a "male" story. Hence my question about whether you think this is an artistic handicap, because I think it is.

>The director has the daughter be so incompetent that she could never figure it out and became old and Matthew had to figure everything out and see her on her deathbed.

no, Murph is the one who solves the equation using the morse code with the quantum data from TARS  sent by Cooper to Murph, if Murph didnt solve the equation, humanity would not have found a solution to the problem

you clearly didnt pay attention

not to mention Murph is the one who saves her sister in law and her child by setting the field on fire to create a distraction so they can escape from Casey Affleck

lol this is a very silly and disingenuous reading that completely ignores the fact that most of the problems in the story are caused by three men

Matt Damon, Casey Affleck and Michael Caines characters

they all lie or ignore evidence for selfish reasons and put people in unnecessary danger

i feel like you're just seeing gender where you conveniently want to, to fit your argument, and then conveniently ignoring it where it doesnt suit you

Murph is a central plot device, but is barely a character. She definitely wasn’t one of the main characters of the movie, Anne Hathaway was much more of a main character but was also very one dimensional. I genuinely can’t think of a single female role nolan has written that’s beyond one dimensional.

Or perhaps the director didn’t paint it as important as what Matthew did. There’s no way of knowing. But personally, I’m not striker by his female characters. They seem to be props. I love films that feature strong women and the director actively agrees to show you. Lady Snowblood, Foxy Brown, La Femme Nikita, The Long Kiss Goodnight, Can You Ever Forgive Me… fully formed human beings. The daughter in Interstellar has slightly more say than Sarah Jessica Parker in Flight of the Navigator.

Incapable is a bit harsh...uninterested is possibly a 5 word. It's clear to me that Nolan is obsessed with a type of masculine character that is extremely driven, competent and sharp dressed but emotionally stunted.
 All he wants to do is to tell stories focused about these kind of characters with female characters mostly used as a complement.
A director that comes to mind with a similar inclination is Michael Mann.
I too thought of Michael Mann

> Or perhaps the director didn’t paint it as important as what Matthew did.

No you just made a mistake and instead of admitting it, you're blaming it on the director. It's like watching Return of the Jedi and forgetting Vader kills the emperor. Her discoveries are treated as a pivotal moment in the film and given focus. There's literally a scene of her solving the equation and shouting "Eureka". Not just that there's a moment in the film when Cooper thinks the space station is named after him and is corrected by others saying it's named after his daughter. All of this is "shown".

> Lady Snowblood, Foxy Brown, La Femme Nikita, The Long Kiss Goodnight, Can You Ever Forgive Me… fully formed human beings. 

Typical of a r/truefilm user to hide behind arthouse/classic films when you can't provide an argument with substance.

First you tried to argue his female characters are "incompetent" and when shown you're shown to be wrong when it comes to interstellar(and you are wrong btw) you pivot to arguing how they're not fleshed out as female characters that are not only main characters in their films but are also from more character driven films than what Nolan usually makes. Amazing.
